messages.author: 3ef7a01c7d912ca2
messages.subject: Lost in 1093-dimensional space
parts:
When reading the 1.3.0 manual for the first time, I was shocked by the ability of stan to handle 1093-dimensional vectors:

For example, a 1093 dimensional row vector u would be declared as row_vector[1093] u; (page 147)

This is far beyond my Einsteinian world is as close to Hilpert-space one can get.

Is there any reason for using "dimensional" here instead of length or size (first part of sentence)?

From Base R Documentation:

An array in R can have one, two or more dimensions. It is simply a vector which is stored with additional attributes giving the dimensions (attribute "dim") and optionally names for those dimensions (attribute "dimnames").

A two-dimensional array is the same thing as a matrix.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: array/vector/matrix terminology for dimensions vs. size vs. length
parts:
Andrew --- you might be the best one to answer this given
our shared love of precise terminology.

On 5/28/13 4:05 AM, Dieter Menne wrote:
> When reading the 1.3.0 manual for the first time, I was shocked by the ability of stan to handle 1093-dimensional vectors:
>
> For example, a 1093 dimensional row vector u would be declared as row_vector[1093] u; (page 147)
>
> This is far beyond my Einsteinian world is as close to Hilpert-space one can get.

I just meant a row vector of size 1093. Nothing is inherently non-Euclidean.
See below.
> Is there any reason for using "dimensional" here instead of length or size (first part of sentence)?

I was trying to be precise. The problem with "length" is
that "length" is also used for the L2 norm. The problem with
size() is that it's non-standard in math, though standard in
C++.

> From Base R Documentation:
>
> An array in *R* can have one, two or more dimensions. It is simply a vector which is stored with additional attributes
> <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/attributes> giving the dimensions (attribute |"dim"|) and optionally

> names for those dimensions (attribute |"dimnames"|).
>

> A two-dimensional array is the same thing as a |matrix <http://127.0.0.1:25263/help/library/base/help/matrix>|.

OK --- I see the problem with the terminology here.

Usually if we have [0.9 1.7 -102.789]', that's a vector representing a
point in 3-dimensional space. 0.9 is the first dimension (x),
1.7 the second dimension (y) and -102.789 the third dimension.

But then people talk about "2D array" when they mean it has two
indices.

You can see the overload in the Wikipedia description of arrays
and vectors:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclidean_vector#Other_dimensions

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_data_structure

I'd like to be consistent and not confuse those used to R, those
used to C++, or those used to mathematical terminology.

But even "vector" is ambiguous between a vector data type and
the mathematical concept of a vector.

I'm thinking we should probably stick to "size" unless someone has
a better suggestion. But then if I have a 1D array of size
10, how do I refer to the third element of the array? Maybe "position"?

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] array/vector/matrix terminology for dimensions vs. size vs. length
parts:
> Which, "size"?

No, dimension.

> Is there some way to remove the ambiguity in "dimensional"
> a 3-dimensional array:
>
> real a[I,J,K];
>
> and a 3-dimensional vector:
>
> vector[3] v;
>
> The vector v is a one-dimensional data structure, but
> a three-dimensional vector. Should we just say that
> v has size 3 and not ever refer to what it has 3 of
> as dimensions? I don't know any alternative terminology
> for a 3-dimensional array like a.

From the math perspective, matrices are just vectors tensored together. So an n by m matrix is order two or rank two (number of vectors tensored together) with dimension n and dimension m (the individual dimensions are specified separately).

Likewise, a[i, j, k] is order 3 (or rank three, if you're comfortable with the overlapping terminology) with dimensions dim(i), dim(j), and dim(k).
